name: Dry brush
lead: Dry brushing, also called dry skin brushing or garshana, is the practice of stroking a stiff, natural-bristle brush over dry skin, usually before a shower, in long strokes directed toward the heart. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, links it to Ayurvedic tradition and to a Japanese practice of dry towel friction [1].

Proponents say it exfoliates dead skin, stimulates circulation, promotes lymphatic drainage, supports detoxification and reduces the appearance of cellulite. The same source says that exfoliation and temporary smoothness and pinkness are generally supported by dermatological experts as direct effects of the mechanical action, while evidence for meaningful lymphatic stimulation, detoxification beyond normal body processes or lasting cellulite reduction is limited or absent [1]. The site's rating is limited, and its outcome category is temporary.
infobox: Ayurvedic garshana; related Japanese kanpu masatsu (per Grokipedia) [1]

paras: The brush used is typically long-handled with firm natural bristles such as boar hair or plant fibres like sisal, and is applied for a few minutes on completely dry skin, without oils or lotions [1]. Brushes with softer bristles are described for sensitive skin and firmer ones for resilient skin; short palm-style brushes allow more precise control [1]. Users commonly follow a session with a shower and moisturiser [1].

Grokipedia says the practice traces to Ayurvedic medicine, where it is called garshana, a Sanskrit term it glosses as friction by rubbing, traditionally performed with raw silk or linen gloves and associated in that tradition with the lymphatic system and the removal of toxins. It also describes a related Japanese practice, kanpu masatsu, popular in the 1940s, and says dry brushing spread in Western wellness culture in the late 20th century through naturopathic and holistic movements [1]. These historical statements come from an AI-generated source and were not independently verified.

Proponents describe the bristles as abrading dead surface cells and briefly increasing blood flow to the skin, producing a pink, smoother look. The lymph-drainage claim rests on the direction of strokes toward the heart and major lymph nodes [1]. Clinical manual lymphatic drainage is a separate, trained technique, and Grokipedia notes dry brushing is sometimes used as a preparatory step before it [1].

No studies found. Searches for dry brushing in the biomedical literature mainly return unrelated results in which dry brush refers to polymer chemistry or to cervical screening sampling brushes, which are not relevant to skin brushing.

Grokipedia reports that dry brushing is considered generally safe for most people when gentle, but that vigorous use or use on compromised skin can cause irritation, redness, abrasions or infection. It lists open wounds, rashes, infections, inflamed areas, sunburn, eczema and psoriasis as situations in which it is contraindicated, advises people with sensitive skin or existing conditions to consult a healthcare provider, and says brushes should be cleaned regularly to prevent bacterial buildup [1].

Dry brushes are discussed as an inexpensive exfoliant. The site's own summary notes that the lymph-drainage claims have limited support. Forum threads retrieved for this entry mention brushes only incidentally (for example back scrubbers and food brushes), so no community-specific claims could be documented.
